title: Citation and plagiarism
note: Cite whenever you use someone else's words, data or ideas, whether you quote, paraphrase or summarize. APA 7 uses author and date: (Jones, 2020, p. 4). MLA 9 uses author and page: (Jones 4). A true paraphrase changes both wording and structure, and still needs a citation.

read.title: Paraphrase or patchwork?
text: Imagine this sentence from a 2021 article by an author named Lee: "Students who space their study sessions over several days remember more than students who study the same amount in one long session." Here are two attempts to use it.

Attempt one: "Students who spread their study sessions across several days recall more than students who study the same amount in a single long session." A few words changed, but the sentence's structure and most of its wording are the source's. That is patchwriting, and many instructors treat it as plagiarism even with a citation.

Attempt two: "Splitting study time into several shorter sessions on different days improves memory more than cramming the same hours into one sitting (Lee, 2021)." The idea is the same, but the wording and structure are new, and the citation credits the idea. That is a genuine paraphrase.

When the exact wording matters, quote instead, with quotation marks and a page number: (Lee, 2021, p. 12) in APA or (Lee 12) in MLA. A practical way to paraphrase well is to read the passage, close the source, write the idea from memory, then check your version against the original for accidental borrowing.

q.q: Why is attempt one a problem?
o: It changes the source's meaning entirely
It keeps the source's structure and most of its wording

q.q: What makes attempt two a genuine paraphrase?
o: New wording and structure, plus a citation
It leaves out the source's idea

q.q: What paraphrasing method does the reading suggest?
o: Replace every third word with a synonym
Close the source, write from memory, then check
Copy the passage, then reorder the clauses
